node.label: Tina Loo
node.date_label: Making Law, Order, and Authority (1994) · Making Good, with Carolyn Strange (1997) · States of Nature (2006) · Moved by the State (2019)
node.description: In States of Nature (2006), Tina Loo argues that Canadian wildlife conservation expanded state authority and marginalized customary uses, while rural people and private organizations remained major conservation actors. Conservation was also a struggle over social values and the remaking of rural Canada. The book won the Canadian Historical Association’s principal book prize in 2007 and the Harold Adams Innis Prize in 2008. Her earlier books include Making Law, Order, and Authority in British Columbia, 1821–1871 (1994). With Carolyn Strange, Making Good (1997) examined law and moral regulation; Christopher English, reviewing it for undergraduate readers, found its survey clear but said the link between the family and the reformers' goals was 'not made explicit.' Moved by the State (2019) examines forced relocation within postwar projects of welfare and development, including the disciplinary effects of participation. Fred Burrill credits its recovery of rural agency but argues that its attention to officials’ intentions misses patterns of white supremacy and gives too little weight to Inuit assessments.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Making Law, Order, and Authority in British Columbia, 1821–1871 (1994); Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada, 1867–1939 (1997), with Carolyn Strange; States of Nature: Conserving Canada’s Wildlife in the Twentieth Century (2006; paperback 2007); “An Environmental History of Progress” (2011), with Meg Stanley; “High Modernism, Conflict, and the Nature of Change in Canada” (2016); Moved by the State: Forced Relocation and Making a Good Life in Postwar Canada (2019).
node.scope_note: States of Nature: publisher metadata, cataloguing leaf and selected introduction passages, pp. 2 and 5–7; Moved by the State: publisher metadata and selected introduction passages, pp. 6–11 and 18. Neither book read in full. Making Good read through Bacchi’s complete review. Loo’s Harris and Valverde reviews read directly; the reviewed books unread. The 2016 Scott intervention is known only through its author abstract; the 2014 essay and the 1994 Brownlie–Kelm exchange remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “High Modernism, Conflict, and the Nature of Change in Canada” (2016), Loo questions the opposition between local knowledge and state expertise in Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher-indexed author abstract, final sentence: “takes issue with Scott’s contention”. Article body returned HTTP 403 and remains unread; this proposal covers only the stated objection.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) in 1998, Loo praises Harris’s account of land and power but criticizes its limited treatment of Indigenous agency and its weakening connections between settlement and colonization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete BC Studies 117 review, pp. 64–67; criticism at pp. 66–67, including “emerge as victims” and “fade away”. Harris’s book was not independently read; the claim is Loo’s assessment.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1992 review of The Age of Light, Soap and Water (1991), Loo asks Valverde for fuller treatment of Protestantism and stronger evidence connecting reform discourse to state practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Labour/Le Travail 30, pp. 277–279, read in the national library’s journal archive; pp. 278–279: “religion and sectarian differences” and “more asserted than proved”. She also values the theoretical intervention. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the introduction to States of Nature (2006), Loo draws on Cronon's argument in 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) that concepts of wilderness place it outside history, and extends the point from wilderness to wild animals.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 2 (PDF leaf 26), paragraph naming Cronon: “the trouble with wilderness”. This is an explicit conceptual resource, not evidence of supervision or personal contact; Cronon’s essay was not reread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Loo explicitly uses Foucault’s distinctions between sovereign and disciplinary power to interpret relocation and the shaping of citizens.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 18 (PDF leaf 18): “to use Michel Foucault’s terms”. The adjoining governmentality discussion credits Timothy Mitchell and Tania Murray Li as well; no exclusive derivation is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Loo and Carolyn Strange coauthored Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada, 1867–1939 (1997).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bacchi’s review, p. 247 heading, and Osgoode Society bibliography, Making Good entry, explicitly credit both authors. Book unread; the proposal asserts coauthorship only. Strange is another candidate in entries.json.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Loo compares her effort to historicize state officials with E. P. Thompson’s recovery of historical actors in The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, printed p. 6 (PDF leaf 6): “my purpose is broadly similar”. This is Loo’s bounded comparison of historical empathy, not an identification of officials with Thompson’s working class or a shared political programme.
proposed_edges.map_label: Compares the recovery of historical actors

proposed_edges.relationship: States of Nature (2006) makes wildlife conservation a history of state authority, competing social values and the continuing importance of private and rural actors.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, introduction pp. 5–7, especially the three arguments on pp. 6–7: “three main arguments”. Selected opening passages read; later chapters unread. Existing environment roster row is retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: Strange and Loo's Making Good (1997), a survey for undergraduates, traces the changing scope and subjects of moral regulation in Canada from 1867 to 1939 and the often ineffective enforcement of moral laws.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Carol Bacchi, Australian Journal of Legal History 4 (1998), pp. 247–249, complete review: “uneven, inconsistent and contradictory” (248); criticism of self-regulation (249). Mediated claim with joint authorship preserved; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Moved by the State (2019) links forced relocation to postwar welfare and development policy, examining how the state’s pursuit of improvement also shaped political subjects.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher sample, introduction pp. 6–8 and 18: “project of improvement” (8). Only these selected argument passages and the publisher description support the proposal; case-study chapters unread. Existing political-history roster retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Moved by the State (2019), Tina Loo examines forced relocation as an expression of the contradictions of extending Canada's liberal order, connecting individual development with coercive state intervention, as Caroline Desbiens explains in her review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Desbiens's complete review on the journal's website. This is a review-supported contribution to the framework's application, not evidence that McKay drew upon Loo. The book itself was not read for this edge. The review is printed in BC Studies 205 (Spring 2020), pp. 110–111; its webpage is dated 17 September 2019.

proposed_edges.relationship: Christopher Douglas Herbert identifies Tina Loo's Making Law, Order, and Authority in British Columbia, 1821–1871 (1994) as an innovative contribution to British Columbia's historiography that makes Cariboo gold-rush society central to understanding the province's development.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal's PDF, especially pp. 17–19. Herbert places Loo's argument within a substantive assessment of provincial historiography and explains the challenge to company authority. This supports a regional-history contribution; it does not establish influence on Barman or Perry, who are discussed separately. The book was not read for this edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Makes the Cariboo central to provincial history

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'The View from Jacob Street: Reframing Urban Renewal in Postwar Halifax' (2019), Tina Loo contributes to urban history by examining municipal power alongside federal redevelopment policy and arguing that both race and class shaped vulnerability to displacement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal-hosted HTML introduction, paragraphs 1–10, and conclusion, paragraphs 75–77. The edge records Loo's stated historiographical intervention, without treating her interpretation of municipal intentions as settled or asserting subsequent uptake by another historian. The journal identifies the article as a 2019 publication.
proposed_edges.map_label: Municipal power, race and class in urban renewal
